title: Loneliness, and whether it is a health problem

turns.speaker: Lin
turns.text: The practice has started prescribing social groups. Actually writing it on a prescription pad, alongside the tablets.

turns.speaker: Otis
turns.text: That sounds like a headline rather than medicine.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: The mortality figures make it harder to dismiss. Persistent loneliness tracks with a risk increase comparable to smoking, in the large reviews.

turns.speaker: Otis
turns.text: Comparable to smoking is a very strong claim.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: It is, and the causal direction is the weak point. Being ill makes you isolated as readily as isolation makes you ill.

turns.speaker: Lin
turns.text: The longitudinal work does point one way more than the other, though. Loneliness at fifty predicts decline at sixty-five better than the reverse.

turns.speaker: Otis
turns.text: Alright, that's more persuasive than the raw correlation.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: What bothers me about prescribing it is that it treats a structural thing as a personal one. The bus route went, the pub shut, the post office closed.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: None of that is fixed by a leaflet about a walking group.

turns.speaker: Lin
turns.text: Except the walking group is what exists this month, and the bus route isn't coming back.

turns.speaker: Otis
turns.text: That's the argument for doing both rather than for doing neither.

turns.speaker: Lin
turns.text: And the evaluations are reasonable. Not dramatic, but fewer appointments and people report feeling better.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: I'd just rather it wasn't the only thing anyone is funded to do.

points: A medical practice has begun prescribing social activities alongside medication.
Cerys cites reviews linking persistent loneliness to mortality risk comparable to smoking.
She acknowledges causal direction is the weakness, since illness also causes isolation.
Lin notes longitudinal evidence that loneliness at fifty predicts later decline better than the reverse.
Cerys objects that social prescribing treats a structural problem, caused by lost buses, pubs and post offices, as an individual one.
Lin and Otis argue for doing both, noting evaluations show modest benefits in wellbeing and fewer appointments.
